column4: While hitting rock-bottom is more a myth than a certain precondition to change, God can use sorrow to influence our minds.  God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes to see our complete and total need of Him.
column5: Although reaching "rock bottom" is more a myth than a prerequisite for change, God can use sorrow to influence our thinking. God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us regarding our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes and show us our complete and absolute need for Him.

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or <u>an experience of grief or suffering that leads to *metanoia*</u>, is not the same as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of grief or suffering, but the world offers no hope, only relief and a promise of death.

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: Suffering is the enduring of pain—physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual—especially when it is prolonged or intense.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to a significant personal loss, especially in relationships or on an existential level.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Sadness, suffering, and grief — are closely related concepts. In our human life we will experience all three; through each of them we can learn and grow, but God will not bring death and destruction into our lives in order to teach us.

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.
column5: Scripture says that every good gift and every perfect gift comes from above, from God (James 1:17). He is — a good Father, Who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will bring discomfort, but His discipline is just and full of love. Just as a good father will not deliberately break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson,’ God will not send sickness or infirmity upon His children to teach us.

column4: ### Example of Worldly Sorrow vs Godly Sorrow
column5: ### An example of worldly sorrow and godly sorrow

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick and deliberately hit her, which made her cry, and a red mark was left on her skin.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Hearing the commotion, their father found out what was going on and, learning what his son had done, took the stick, broke it in half, and threw it away. He sent the son into the house to think about what he had done, and comforted the daughter.

column4: The father coming inside to deal with his son found him crying. Asking him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.
column5: When the father came in to talk with the son, he found him in tears. In answer to the question of why he was crying, the son replied: "because you broke my stick".

column4: The father’s reply was, “I’m sad that you are more concerned about your stick than you are about your sister who you hurt” and sent him back to his room for more reflection.
column5: The father answered: "I am sad that you care more about your stick than about your sister whom you hurt" and sent him back to the room for further reflection.

column4: A few minutes later his son came back out and apologized. He said he was still sad because dad has broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.
column5: After a few minutes the son came out and apologized. He said that he was still sad because Dad had broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.

column4: **Progress!**
column5: **Progress!**

column4: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow, for his lost stick, and then eventually godly sorrow, for his hurt sister.
column5: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow — because of the lost stick, — and, in the end, godly sorrow — because of the pain caused to his sister.

column4: Godly sorrow and God’s goodness are connected. God is a good father that will let us experience the consequences of our actions but will still stand beside us as we walk through those consequences.
column5: Godly sorrow is connected with God’s goodness. God is — a good Father, who will allow us to experience the consequences of our actions, but will still stand by when we go through these consequences.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: God’s unfailing goodness — His willingness to redeem and restore us when we come to Him — is a positive factor on our path of repentance. His goodness is not that we should continue to sin, but that, in spite of our sin, He opens the way to our redemption and lets us experience His salvation.

In the extreme opposite, for some people the mere example of sin and consequence in someone else’s life is enough to cause them to change their thinking.

column4: Man has great capacity to change; it's wired into our very essence. Humans are very adaptable, we can learn and grow, and find better ways to do things. However, a capacity to change is not the same as a willingness or a persuasion to change.
column5: A human being has a tremendous capacity for change; it is built into our very nature. People are highly adaptable: we can learn and grow, and find better ways of doing things. However, the ability to change — is not the same as the willingness or conviction to change.

column4: I do not know why some people get stuck and others are so ready to change, but I can say that the entire process of change is really from God’s grace.

column4: The process of repentance begins before we accept Jesus as our personal Lord and Savior, but the lifestyle of repentance is to endure for our entire Christian walk. We are to throw off dead works and change our minds away from them to the truth of God.
column5: The process of repentance begins even before we receive Jesus as our personal Lord and Savior, but the lifestyle of repentance should continue throughout our Christian journey. We must renounce dead works and turn our minds from them to God’s truth.

column4: Repentance can be a purely natural process, but repentance is also the work of the Spirit calling out to us, opening our eyes to the truth, changing our hearts, beckoning us to be transformed. Galatians 6:1 reminds us that some will be ‘stuck’ in a trespass (sin) and need help to get unstuck! That help comes in the form of mature men and women who help restore us in a spirit of gentleness.
column5: Repentance can be a purely natural process, but repentance is also the work of the Spirit, who calls out to us, opens our eyes to the truth, changes our hearts, calling us to transformation. Galatians 6:1 reminds us that some will find themselves ‘stuck’ in a transgression (sin) and need help to get out! That help comes in the form of mature men and women who help restore us in a spirit of gentleness.

column4: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent for change mankind can engage with, and this is backed up by both the scriptures and by research. Research by “Lyons et al. column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s Example of Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps no account in Scripture provides a more vivid example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin as recorded in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to war and seeing Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing that she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba becoming pregnant.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To conceal his actions, David summons Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child’s father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go home to Bathsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines, where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah’s death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to hide the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was displeased with David’s actions and sends the prophet Nathan to rebuke him. When the prophet rebuked him, David immediately admitted: “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This admission was the first step of his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly before God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51 David’s words, “*For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his full ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only over the sin itself but over having offended God, saying: “*Against You, You only, have I sinned.*” David displayed a “*broken and contrite heart,*” which is a necessary part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow was not superficial; he deeply mourned the sin committed and the pain caused. Such depth of remorse was a sign that he desired not only forgiveness but a changed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David asked God: “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would keep him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than simply asking for forgiveness, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying: “*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He understood that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire for spiritual renewal reflects a sincere resolve to continue walking in God’s ways. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) shows his hope to be aligned with God in every area of his life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Although God forgave David his sin, the Lord struck the child, and he became gravely ill. David fasted, prayed, and begged God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we find both a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his offenses. David’s decision to record his plea for mercy, creating one of the most famous psalms in the Bible, shows his willingness to be open about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony to repentance and restoration from which others could learn, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s path of repentance was not merely a feeling of regret; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and heart transformation as described in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson about God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the most significant biblical examples of genuine repentance.
